 TV Shows Published November 11, 2026 'VisionQuest’ Creator Terry Matalas Breaks Down That Emotional Finale and James Spader’s Dance Skills 
 The showrunner goes behind the scenes of the final episode, from that “Rhinestone Cowboy” needle drop to the long-awaited Maximoff family reunion. 
 BY Devan Coggan Warning: This article contains spoilers for the VisionQuest   finale. 
 >PROGRAM: VISIONQUEST [FINAL SEQUENCE COMPLETE…]  
 Marvel Television’s VisionQuest  ends with an unlikely — and emotional — family reunion.
 All season long, Paul Bettany’s  Vision has been grappling with his past and his programming, facing off against his father-figure Ultron ( James Spader ) and reconnecting with his son Tommy Shepherd ( Ruaridh Mollica ). The eighth and final episode (streaming now on Disney+) has Vision coming face to face with the mysterious client who’s been haunting his steps all season: Virgil Horton. Played by a flamboyant and mustachioed Spader, Virgil is a wealthy tech entrepreneur and descendant of the inventor Phineas Horton, who built the original Synthetic Man , Jim Hammond . Pieces of Jim’s code live on in Ultron, Vision, and every A.I. that shares their programming, making for a complicated family legacy. 
 “Terry [Matalas] and I talked a lot of about Virgil, right up until the last minute,” Spader tells Marvel.com. “We knew a couple of things that were crucial, and that was that he should be nothing like what you would expect. He should be the opposite of what your intuition would tell you. He should be as dichotomous as Ultron, just as dangerous as Ultron, just as childlike and mercurial as Ultron, and yet completely different from Ultron. The one thing he’s completely lacking is any sort of gravitas, and Ultron is just oozing gravitas.” 
 “Virgil’s also not really the final obstacle,” Matalas adds. “He really couldn’t be because the story is about Vision and Ultron and Tommy. So what’s great is you meet this mystery villain, and then Ultron squashes him like a bug and then becomes the real final boss, if you will.” 
 In the end, Ultron easily dispatches Virgil, and what tips the genocidal android over the edge isn’t his hatred of mankind or his maniacal desire for power. It’s the loss of Jocasta ( T’Nia Miller ), the fellow A.I. he’d developed feelings for. Ultimately, the finale sets up a showdown between Ultron and Vision, as Vision tries to convince Ultron to reconnect with his humanity — with an assist from Vision’s reunited sons Tommy and Billy ( Joe Locke, reprising his role from Agatha All Along ).
 “Emotion is the catalyst to Ultron becoming the ultimate bad guy again and the battle with his own son,” Spader adds. “How do you get there? It wasn’t through violence but because of emotion and the loss of this person who he’d fallen in love with.” 
 Of course, this is VisionQuest , so the show couldn’t end without a few final surprises — including a trippy sitcom journey into Ultron’s mind and a wild dance sequence set to Glen Campbell’s “Rhinestone Cowboy.” Below, Matalas unlocks the secrets of the finale, from Spader’s dance skills to the emotional reunion between Vision, Billy, and Tommy. 
 MARVEL.COM: We’ve gotta start by talking about “Rhinestone Cowboy.” Tell me everything about how that scene came together and why that was the perfect song choice. 
 TERRY MATALAS:  You know, a lot of the music in the show were songs that my father used to play on road trips. There was “Rhinestone Cowboy,” there was John Denver’s “Calypso,” “The Last Farewell” by Roger Whittaker, which ends the show. To channel that father and son energy, I was putting that in. 
 Also, it’s an unexpected song to have an action scene to. It’s unexpected and a little weird, and I think unexpected and weird is definitely me. Then, it was getting to get Spader to do a little dance to that song with T’Nia. Hopefully the audience will like it because we had fun making it. 
 MARVEL.COM: What do you remember most about shooting that dance sequence?  
 TERRY MATALAS: Just how much we were all laughing behind the monitors. Getting Spader to dance was not something we ever expected to do. But at that point, he was having so much fun, and we were like, “Let’s try it and see what happens.” We ended up burning almost half the day just shooting that dance. And T’Nia is actually a wonderful dancer, so filming her as she was being controlled, it was just great. 
 MARVEL.COM: There’s an amazing sequence in the finale where Vision pulls Ultron into a sitcom world called UltraVision , and it’s a great callback to the fake TV world of WandaVision . Why did you want to incorporate that sitcom element into the finale? 
 TERRY MATALAS:  I think all good endings always touch upon the beginning in some way. Certainly, WandaVision  was the beginning of all this. It was also a way to get these characters in a room to talk about their feelings in an unexpected way, which is really what television is all about. 
 There’s the expected final conflict, which is like Rock’em Sock’em Robots, which we had to deliver. I wanted to give the Marvel popcorn there. But I also wanted the final conflict to be something really unexpected. It hasn’t aired yet, so we’ll see what people think of it. 
 MARVEL.COM: It sort of speaks to the ethos of this show. It can be unexpected and humorous — but also really heartfelt and moving. 
 TERRY MATALAS:  I mean, that’s the core of a really good sitcom, when it does exactly that. 
 MARVEL.COM: The final episode reunites Billy and Tommy with their father Vision. How did you want to approach that family reunion?  
 TERRY MATALAS:  I wanted it to feel earned. That was the tricky thing: We knew Billy was out there looking for [Tommy], but we wanted to give Billy limitations. He’s a young warlock trying to figure out how to do all this, and sure, he’s got Agatha in his head telling him what to do, but can he actually do it? So getting them together and seeing them be brothers for the first time is really fun. 
 But also, how is he going to get from Westview to London? Does he have those capabilities? He’s not Doctor Strange , but can he be at the right moment? Hopefully by the time we do reunite that family, it’s this incredible emotional catharsis. 
 MARVEL.COM: I also wanted to ask about the seventh episode, where Vision learns that he shares code with Jim Hammond, the original Synthetic Man . You have a great scene where Paul Bettany simultaneously plays Vision, Jim, and Jim’s creator Phineas Horton. How was it shooting that sequence with three Paul Bettanys? 
 TERRY MATALAS:  I mean, incredible. Paul has just been the best collaborator. In that scene in particular, we were united on what it needed to be from the very beginning. There was a built-up pressure on it, certainly as to writing it. I don’t know that I wrote anything more than that scene. Then, Paul and I continued to refine it, even on the day. 
 I loved his take on Phineas. I loved his take on Jim. And there’s the breakdown, this key moment of [Vision] breaking down and admitting the feelings of loss that he has for the Maximoff family and for Wanda. There was a lot of pressure for both Paul and I to get that right. But what could have been a really hard day ended up being a wonderful day of us just continuing to refine it and make it great.
 Paul, he was making everybody cry that day. We only did the actual breakdown three times, I think, and we had it by the first take. We were all crying behind the camera watching. He’s so good. 
 MARVEL.COM: Jim Hammond has such an interesting history in Marvel Comics as the original Human Torch. Why did you want to bring him into VisionQuest ? 
 TERRY MATALAS:  Well, this is the show about the Marvel A.I.s and the robots, right? And he was the first one in Marvel lore. You can see him behind glass — or a version of him, at least — behind glass in Captain America: The First Avenger . It’s the idea of going into family trauma and well, where did Vision get his face from? He didn’t get it from Edwin Jarvis. Where did he get that voice from? The idea that it actually went back to the 1920s was really fun.
 It’s a family story, the idea that this whole family was connected in some way from Phineas to Jim to Phineas’ daughter to Virgil. They all carried bits of DNA into who Vision and Ultron were.
 Marvel Television’s  VisionQuest   is streaming now, exclusively on Disney+.
